traveler: Njall Thorgeirsson of Bergthorshvoll, called Burnt Njal (Brennu-Njall)
title: The Beardless Lawyer of the Landeyjar: Njal, the Law, and the Burning at Bergthorshvoll
years: c. 935 - c. 1011 (the saga's own reckoning); the saga written 1270-1290
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Nidaros, the king's errandmen
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the saga gives no date and names no Norwegian place, and Nidaros stands here for the royal Norway the family leaves. Sources disagree on the dead man's name. Wikipedia 'Njall Thorgeirsson' makes him Ofeigr, father of Thorgeir gollnir; Dasent ch. 20 reads 'Thorgeir Gelling, the son of Thorolf'.
stops.campa: Njal's grandfather falls out of favour with the king of Norway and lays plans to take ship west. The king's errandmen reach him before the weather does and take his life where he stands. His widow gathers the children and sails for Iceland without him, and a family that will be famous for law begins in a killing that no law answered. The saga names neither the fjord nor the year. It gives the emigration and the reason for it. Of Norway itself the saga gives nothing.
suggested_refs: The settlement-era emigration from Norway to Iceland, c. 870-930, as narrated in Landnamabok
sources: The Story of Burnt Njal, tr. George Webbe Dasent, 1861, ch. 20

stops.name: Bergthorshvoll, the knoll in the Landeyjar
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no birth year for Njal survives anywhere, and c. 935 is back-calculated from the burning. Coordinate per Wikipedia 'Bergthorshvoll' (63 deg 38'10 N, 20 deg 19'48 W), in Vestur-Landeyjar on the west bank of the Affall; the research pool's 63.7561 / -20.2419 is the modern town of Hvolsvollur, 13.5 km away.
stops.campa: Njal Thorgeirsson holds a farm on a low knoll in the Landeyjar, on the western bank of the Affall, where the land flattens toward the black southern coast and a rider is visible for miles before he arrives. Asgerda is his mother. He keeps a second homestead at Thorolfsfell in the hills, but Bergthorshvoll is the house that will carry his name into every century after his. The turf walls and long roof timbers standing here now will be his tomb, and the whole island will learn the shape of them.
suggested_refs: The mound of Bergthorshvoll in Vestur-Landeyjar, west bank of the Affall river
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 20

stops.name: Bergthorshvoll, the lawyer without a beard
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the saga introduces Njal as already established and gives no year. The character sketch is Dasent ch. 20, verbatim.
stops.campa: Men ride to the knoll from every quarter of the south with their disputes half-formed and ride home knowing what the law will say. Njal is wealthy in goods and handsome of face, and no beard grows on his chin. He is foreknowing: he sees how a case will run, and how a killing will run, years before either happens. He gives counsel freely and never gives it wrong. The saga sets him down at once as the wisest man in Iceland. A hundred chapters later the men of his own household burn inside it with him.
stops.quote: Njal was wealthy in goods, and handsome of face; no beard grew on his chin. He was so great a lawyer, that his match was not to be found. Wise too he was, and foreknowing and foresighted. Of good counsel, and ready to give it, and all that he advised men was sure to be the best for them to do.
stops.quote_source: The Story of Burnt Njal, tr. Dasent, 1861, ch. 20 (Project Gutenberg #597)
suggested_refs: Dasent's chapter 20, the saga's introductory character-sketch of Njal
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 20

stops.name: Bergthorshvoll, Bergthora and the children
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no year survives for the marriage or for any birth in the household.
stops.campa: He marries Bergthora Skarphedinsdottir, high-spirited, brave-hearted, and hard-tempered, a woman who answers an insult the same day it is given. Six children come of it: Skarphedinn, who grins before he kills, then Grim, then Helgi, and three daughters. Hrodny bears him a base-born son, Hoskuld. The household on the knoll is large and quick to take offence. Its master will spend his life settling other men's feuds, and the feud that kills him starts at his own table.
suggested_refs: The genealogy of Njal's household, Dasent chs. 20-25
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 20-21, 25

stops.name: Thingvellir, the dower of Unnur
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no year survives. Coordinate is the corpus's canonical Thingvellir pin, inherited from william_morris.journey.json. Wikipedia 'Logberg' states the exact site of the Law-Rock is unknown, with at least three candidates (Hallurinn, Almannagja, Hestagja), the rift valley having shifted in a thousand years.
stops.campa: Gunnar Hamundarson rides to the knoll for advice: Unnur's dower is held by Hrut and no straightforward suit will pry it loose. Njal gives him a device, and Gunnar carries it to the Law-Rock in the rift valley where the whole island meets each summer to make and unmake fortunes by procedure. The device works and Hrut pays. From that summer the two men are bound, the greatest fighter in Iceland and the man who never lifts a weapon. The saga's first half runs on that friendship and ends when it does.
suggested_refs: The Logberg and the assembly plain of Thingvellir, seat of the Althing from 930
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 21-22

stops.name: Hlidarendi, the friendship and the servants' feud
stops.date_confidence: traditional, sequence date only: no year survives. Coordinate per Wikipedia 'Hlidarendi' (63 deg 43'29 N, 19 deg 57'02 W); the research pool's 63.6989 / -19.9528 sits 2.9 km south, off the Fljotshlid slope and in the floodplain. The site today carries a church and churchyard and remains an occupied farm, not turf ruins.
stops.campa: Gunnar's farm sits on the green shoulder of Fljotshlid, looking south across the plain to the sea. He and Njal exchange counsel, gifts, and sons, and hold to each other while their wives do not. Bergthora and Hallgerdur trade killings of servants back and forth for years, each answering the last, and after every death the two husbands meet, name a price in silver, and stay friends. Njal sees the deaths coming before they arrive. He tells Thord Freedmanson, his sons' foster-father, that a fetch is walking behind him.
stops.quote: "Thou must be a 'fey' man," says Njal, "and thou must have seen the fetch that follows thee, and now be ware of thyself."
stops.quote_source: The Story of Burnt Njal, tr. Dasent, 1861, ch. 41 (Gutenberg #597)
suggested_refs: The farm and churchyard of Hlidarendi on the Fljotshlid slope
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 19, 35-45

stops.name: Bergthorshvoll, the beardless carle
stops.date_confidence: traditional, sequence date only: the insults run across many chapters and no year is given for any of them.
stops.campa: Hallgerdur has found the one thing about Njal that money cannot settle: he has no beard. She calls him the beardless carle and his sons dung-beardlings, and the words travel the district faster than any lawsuit. Bergthora answers in kind, reminding her that Thorvald was not beardless and was murdered by his wife regardless. The insults cost nothing and cannot be compensated at the Thing, and they outlast every settlement the two households ever pay each other.
stops.quote: "That's true," says Bergthora, "yet neither of us finds fault with the other for it; but Thorwald, thy husband, was not beardless, and yet thou plottedst his death."
stops.quote_source: The Story of Burnt Njal, tr. Dasent, 1861, ch. 35 (Gutenberg #597)
suggested_refs: The exchange of insults between Bergthora and Hallgerdur, Dasent chs. 35-44
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 35, 41

stops.name: Stora-Dimon, the watchtower of the plain
stops.date_confidence: attested as geography, traditional as narrative: the hill's identity and location are certain, its role in the saga's chases is the text's own placement.
stops.campa: A single steep hill stands out of the flat river plain between Fljotshlid and the Landeyjar, visible from every farm for miles. Riders use it to judge distance: how far they have come, how far a pursuer is behind. The saga's chases pass and repass it, and men on its slope can see armed parties moving hours before they arrive. In a country with no walls and no forts, sight-lines are the fortification. Whoever stands on this rock at the right hour knows about a killing before the men below it do.
suggested_refs: Stora-Dimon rising from the Markarfljot outwash plain
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 63, 92

stops.name: Markarfljot, Thrain Sigfusson on the ice
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no year survives, and the coordinate is an approximate point on the Markarfljot crossing. The research pool assigned Dasent chs. 92-93 to a 'Grjota ford in Rangarvellir'; Grjota is Thrain's farm in Fljotshlid, and those chapters narrate this killing on the river ice, not ford ambushes.
stops.campa: Thrain Sigfusson has sheltered a man who killed one of Njal's servants and will not answer for it. Njal's sons catch him crossing the Markarfljot on the ice, and Skarphedinn comes down the frozen river with such speed on the slick surface that he strikes before Thrain can turn. He splits the man's skull and never breaks stride. Njal buys the peace afterward with silver and with a stranger gesture: he takes Thrain's son Hoskuld into his own house to raise, and comes to love him better than his own sons.
suggested_refs: The Markarfljot in winter, between Fljotshlid and the Landeyjar
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 92-93

stops.name: Thingvellir, the atonement for Gunnar
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no year survives. The quoted line is Dasent ch. 69, 'Olaf the Peacock's Gifts to Gunnar'; the research pool cited ch. 70, which is wrong in both Gutenberg #597 and sagadb.org, each running to 158 chapters.
stops.campa: Gunnar has killed too often. The Thing sentences him to three years abroad, and Njal negotiates the terms himself, holding the settlement together with money and procedure when both sides would rather have blood. He says openly what he believes: a man taking law against another breaks no peace, because law is the material the country is built out of. Every death in the saga so far has been paid for in silver under that rule. It has worked for fifty years. It will work for perhaps two more.
stops.quote: "That is no breach of settlement," says Njal, "that any man should take the law against another; for with law shall our land be built up and settled, and with lawlessness wasted and spoiled."
stops.quote_source: The Story of Burnt Njal, tr. Dasent, 1861, ch. 69 (Gutenberg #597)
suggested_refs: The most quoted sentence in Icelandic literature, Dasent ch. 69
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 69, 73

stops.name: Markarfljot ford, the turning back
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no document places the stumble at any specific ford, and the crossing point is inferred from the valley's geography. The point lies about 5 km south of and below Hlidarendi; the research pool described it as 'above' the farm, which reverses the direction of Gunnar's ride to the coast.
stops.campa: Njal has told him plainly what the terms hold: keep the atonement, come home in three years to greater honour, grow old with no man treading on his heel. Riding down toward the ship, Gunnar's horse stumbles at the crossing and throws him forward, and he comes up facing back at his own hillside. The slope is fair. He has never seen it so fair, the corn pale and the meadows mown. He turns the horse and rides home to break the sentence. Nothing compels him. The saga stakes its central death on a man looking over his shoulder at grass.
stops.quote: "Take good care, messmate, that thou keepest to this atonement, and bear in mind what we have spoken about; for though thy former journey abroad brought thee to great honour, this will be a far greater honour to thee. Thou wilt come back with great glory, and live to be an old man, and no man here will then tread on thy heel; but if thou dost not fare away, and so breakest thy atonement, then thou wilt be slain here in the land, and that is ill knowing for those who are thy friends."
stops.quote_source: The Story of Burnt Njal, tr. Dasent, 1861, ch. 73 (Gutenberg #597)
suggested_refs: The ford of the Markarfljot below Hlidarendi, where Gunnar turned his horse
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 73, 75

stops.name: Hlidarendi, the bowstring
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no firm date survives; conventionally placed shortly before Iceland's conversion. The research pool dated Gunnar's death to 990 in one lens and the ford stumble to c. 992 in another, which reverses cause and effect; both are placed at c. 990 here and the conflict is recorded, not resolved.
stops.campa: Forty men come for Gunnar at his farm and he holds them off alone from inside the house, shooting until his bowstring parts. He asks Hallgerdur for two locks of her hair to twist a new string. She asks whether his life depends on it. He says it does. She reminds him of the slap he gave her once, and refuses. They tear the roof off and kill him. Njal, hearing of it at Bergthorshvoll, has lost the one counterweight to every enemy he has made in fifty years of other men's lawsuits.
suggested_refs: The killing of Gunnar at Hlidarendi, Dasent chs. 75-77
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 75-77

segments.name: The Law Takes the New Faith

stops.name: Birsay, Orkney: Kari in the earl's service
stops.date_confidence: traditional: c. 995 is a conventional placement. Coordinate per Wikipedia 'Birsay' (59 deg 08.0 N, 3 deg 18.1 W); the research pool's -3.3383 falls about 2 km offshore. Birsay is traditionally rather than documentarily associated with Earl Sigurd, and Njals saga puts the Yule feast on Hrossey.
stops.campa: Helgi and Grim Njalsson, trading in the British Isles, fall into trouble at sea and are pulled out of it by Kari Solmundarson, who takes them into the household of Jarl Sigurd of Orkney. The three winter in the earl's hall among men who will be dead at Clontarf within twenty years. Kari comes back to Iceland with them, marries their sister Helga, and settles at Bergthorshvoll. He has walked into the one house in Iceland that will burn with its people inside, and he is the only man who will walk back out of it.
suggested_refs: The earldom of Orkney under Sigurd Hlodvisson, and its Icelandic retainers

stops.name: Thingvellir, the law takes the faith
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event, disputed in year: Njals saga gives 999, Islendingabok and mainstream historical dating give 1000. This is the only specific year the saga supplies anywhere. Njal's personal presence and stance are the saga's addition to an independently documented assembly.
stops.campa: Thangbrand's preaching has split the island, and the two parties come armed to the assembly, each ready to declare itself out from under the other's law. The lawspeaker lies down under a cloak for a day and a night and comes back with a ruling: one law for the country, and that law Christian, with the old rites permitted in private. Njal is counted among those who favour the new faith. This is the only year the saga dates. Everything else in the life of the wisest lawyer in Iceland floats free of the calendar.
suggested_refs: Ari Thorgilsson's account of the conversion, Islendingabok ch. 7
sources: Ari Thorgilsson, Islendingabok, ch. 7 (cited at one remove)
Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 100

stops.name: Kirkjubaer on the Sida, the church before the church
stops.date_confidence: attested for the papar tradition (Landnamabok); the farm's specific role in Njal's story is saga embroidery and no year attaches to it.
stops.campa: East along the coast under the Sida cliffs stands a farm that already carried a church in its name before any Norseman here was baptized. Irish hermits, the papar, held it before the settlement, and the name outlived them. The new faith moves through the south the way news moves, farm by farm, arriving in most places well before the law arrives. Kirkjubaer is where the country's two Christianities, the one that was here first and the one voted in at the Thing, stand on the same piece of ground.
suggested_refs: Landnamabok on the papar and the church-names of the Sida
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 100

stops.name: Keldur, the turf hall and the tunnel
stops.date_confidence: attested site with a saga-attested occupant: Wikipedia 'Keldur' names Ingjald Hoskuldsson as first recorded occupant and a character in Njals saga, dates the dwelling's foundation to the 11th century, and reports the jardhus tunnel rediscovered in a 1998 excavation. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 63.7756 / -20.0206, which is 5.8 km off, and the pool's claim that Keldur is unnamed in the saga is false.
stops.campa: Ingjald Hoskuldsson farms at Keldur in Rangarvellir, kin by marriage to men who will burn Bergthorshvoll, and when he is asked to ride with them he will refuse. The house he keeps is built as they all are: turf on stone, low against the wind, with a tunnel driven from the floor of the dwelling out to the stream, so that a family can leave a burning hall without going through its door. The household on the flat land below has no such passage. The saga assumes both facts and comments on neither.
suggested_refs: The turf farmstead of Keldur and its jardhus tunnel, rediscovered 1998
sources: Thjodminjasafn Islands survey notes on Keldur farm

stops.name: Ossabaer, the chieftaincy made out of nothing
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no year survives, and Ossabaer's exact site is unlocated. It lies in the Landeyjar within a morning's ride of Bergthorshvoll; the coordinate is approximate. The research pool's 63.85 / -20.4 sits 24 km north in the Rangarvellir or Holt district, which breaks the saga's own geography.
stops.campa: Njal has raised Thrain's son as his own and now sets him up: a farm at Ossabaer a short ride from the knoll, a marriage to Hildigunn who is Flosi's niece, and a chieftaincy conjured at the Thing because every existing one is taken. Hoskuld Hvitanessgodi is generous, mild, and universally liked. The old man has spent his authority to make a godi out of the son of a man his own sons killed on the river ice, and believes he has closed the last open wound in the district.
suggested_refs: The godord of Hvitanes, created at the Althing for Hoskuld Thrainsson
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 94-98

stops.name: Ossabaer, the killing in the corn
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged: the research pool's chronology lens dates this to 1006, its geography lens to c. 1011. The conventional chronology places the killing in the spring immediately before the Althing session and the autumn burning of 1011, which is the reading used here. His title is Hvitanessgodi, godi of Hvitanes, not of the Hvita district as the pool had it.
stops.campa: Mord Valgardsson, who wants the chieftaincy and cannot have it while Hoskuld lives, spends months telling Njal's sons that Hoskuld means to kill them. They ride out before dawn with Mord and find him sowing his field in a scarlet cloak Flosi gave him. He is unarmed. He asks what they mean by this, and then, as they cut him down, asks God to forgive them and to help him. Skarphedinn has killed the one man in Iceland whose death his father cannot pay for, and knows it before the body is cold.
suggested_refs: The killing of Hoskuld Hvitanessgodi in his own field, Dasent ch. 111
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 111

stops.name: Thingvellir, the cloak on the silver
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged: the research pool's chronology lens dates the failed settlement to 1010 and the killing that caused it to 1006, while its geography lens places both in 1011. The Althing session must follow the spring killing, so both are placed in 1011 here.
stops.campa: Njal offers self-judgment and the greatest compensation ever paid in Iceland: silver heaped on the ground at the assembly, three times the ordinary man-price, everyone in the country contributing. Then he lays a silk cloak and a pair of boots on top of the pile. Flosi asks who gave the cloak and no one answers, and he takes the silence and the gift together as a charge that he is unmanly. He kicks the money apart. Both sides leave the Thing with nothing settled, and the law has failed in front of the whole country.
suggested_refs: The heap of silver and the silk cloak at the Althing, Dasent chs. 123-124
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 119-124

stops.name: Thrihyrningur, the burners assemble
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Coordinate per is.wikipedia 'Thrihyrningur (fjall)' (63 deg 47'11 N, 19 deg 58'26 W, 678 m); the research pool's 63.66 / -20.04 sits 14 km south on the outwash plain, and assigned the mountain to Gunnar's kinsmen in chs. 63-64 rather than to the burners of chs. 127-130.
stops.campa: Flosi Thordarson rides west from Svinafell with a hundred men, and they gather in the folds of Thrihyrningshalsar under the three-peaked mountain, where a body of armed riders can be kept out of sight of the entire plain until the hour it is wanted. Hildigunn has already thrown her dead husband's clotted cloak over Flosi's shoulders and called on him by all his manhood to answer for it. From the ridge they can see the smoke of the farms below, and the knoll they mean to reach after dark.
suggested_refs: Thrihyrningshalsar, the ridges where Flosi's hundred waited out the daylight
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 116, 127-130

stops.name: Bergthorshvoll, a hundred men at the door
stops.date_confidence: traditional: c. 1011 is a scholarly convention, not independently attested outside the saga. Coordinate is Bergthorshvoll's true position in Vestur-Landeyjar, not the research pool's Hvolsvollur reading.
stops.campa: They come at dusk and surround the house, a hundred against thirty. Skarphedinn wants to fight outside, where the Njalssons have never lost, and Njal orders them all indoors, reasoning that the walls held once before and that Flosi will not dare burn a household. It is the first counsel of his life that is wrong, and his sons obey it because he has never been wrong. Flosi tries the door, loses men to it, and calls for fire. As the roof takes, the old man's voice comes out through the smoke.
stops.quote: "Is Flosi so near that he can hear my voice." ... "Wilt thou," said Njal, "take an atonement from my sons, or allow any men to go out."
stops.quote_source: The Story of Burnt Njal, tr. Dasent, 1861, ch. 128 (Gutenberg #597)
suggested_refs: Dasent's chapter 128, 'Njal's Burning'
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 128

stops.name: Bergthorshvoll, Njal will not go out
stops.date_confidence: attested within the saga, quoted verbatim from Dasent ch. 128; the research pool cited ch. 129 for this and for every other passage of the burning, which is wrong in Gutenberg #597 and sagadb.org alike.
stops.campa: With the roof alight Flosi offers the women, the children, and the servants free passage, and then, separately, offers it to Njal himself for the honour of his age. Njal asks whether Flosi will take atonement from the sons or let any of them out. Flosi will not. So Njal will not go out either. Bergthora, offered the same, says she was given to him young and promised that they would share one fate, and neither of them raises the matter again. The offer is made twice more and refused twice more.
stops.quote: "I will not go out," said Njal, "for I am an old man, and little fitted to avenge my sons, but I will not live in shame."
stops.quote_source: The Story of Burnt Njal, tr. Dasent, 1861, ch. 128 (Gutenberg #597)
suggested_refs: Bergthora's refusal, spoken in the same chapter: 'I was given away to Njal young'
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 128

stops.name: Bergthorshvoll, the ox-hide
stops.date_confidence: attested within the saga, quoted verbatim from Dasent ch. 128. The child under the hide is Thord Karason, Kari's son and Njal's grandson.
stops.campa: Bergthora carries Kari's small son Thord to the bed. The boy has been told he will not be burned, and says his grandmother promised it. Njal calls the steward, tells him to mark where they lie down and how he lays them out so that afterward men will know where to look for their bones, and has an ox-hide spread over the three of them. They sign themselves and the child with the cross and give their souls into God's hand. Those are the last words anybody outside hears from inside that house.
stops.quote: "Now thou shalt see where we lay us down, and how I lay us out, for I mean not to stir an inch hence, whether reek or burning smart me, and so thou wilt be able to guess where to look for our bones."
stops.quote_source: The Story of Burnt Njal, tr. Dasent, 1861, ch. 128 (Gutenberg #597)
suggested_refs: The ox-hide spread over Njal, Bergthora, and the boy Thord Karason
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 128

stops.name: Bergthorshvoll, Kari on the burning beam
stops.date_confidence: attested within the saga: Wikipedia 'Njals saga' has Kari escape 'under cover of the smoke by running along the beam', and gives eleven dead in total. The research pool's chronology lens both overcounted the dead (Njal and Bergthora 'and about eleven others') and placed Helgi in the fire; he was beheaded outside it.
stops.campa: The cross-beam of the hall is burning end to end, and Kari Solmundarson runs out along it with his hair and clothes alight, drops through the smoke beyond the wall, and rolls in the wet grass until the fire on his back is out. The besiegers see a shape come down in the smoke and take it for a falling timber. He walks away in the dark. Eleven people die in the house. Helgi Njalsson, who tried to leave in a woman's cloak, is beheaded by Flosi in the yard. Skarphedinn burns standing.
suggested_refs: Kari's escape along the cross-beam, Dasent ch. 129
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 128-129

stops.name: Bergthorshvoll, the bodies under the hide
stops.date_confidence: attested within the saga, quoted verbatim from Dasent ch. 131, 'Njal's and Bergthora's Bones Found'; the research pool cited ch. 132.
stops.campa: Men come to the ashes to search, and lift the hide, and the three bodies beneath it are unburned. Bergthora looks as she looked living. Hjallti Skeggjason, asked to say what he sees, says he has never seen any dead man's body as bright as Njal's. They carry the bones away for burial. From that hour nobody in the south speaks of the burning as a killing with a price on it; they speak of it as a martyrdom. Every killing that comes after in the saga answers to it.
stops.quote: Then Hjallti said, "I shall speak what I say with all freedom of speech. The body of Bergthora looks as it was likely she would look, and still fair; but Njal's body and visage seem to me so bright that I have never seen any dead man's body so bright as this."
stops.quote_source: The Story of Burnt Njal, tr. Dasent, 1861, ch. 131 (Gutenberg #597)
suggested_refs: The finding of the unburnt bodies, Dasent ch. 131
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 131

segments.name: Kari's Vengeance and the Battle at Clontarf

stops.name: Thingvellir, the suit that breaks into fighting
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the year follows the conventional dating of the burning to 1011 and is not independently attested.
stops.campa: The case against the burners is brought and argued for days, procedure against procedure, until Mord's summons is challenged on a technicality and the whole court fractures. Thorhall Asgrimsson, lying sick in his booth, hears that the suit is lost, tears the spear out of his own infected leg, and comes onto the field, and the assembly turns into a battle. It is settled at last by arbitration: fines, outlawries, no verdict. Njal spent his life on this instrument and it cannot judge his death.
suggested_refs: The Althing session of the burning case, Dasent chs. 138-145
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 138-145

stops.name: The Eyjafjoll coast, the outlaws take ship
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the embarkation point is not named precisely enough in the text to fix beyond this general coast.
stops.campa: Sentenced to outlawry, Flosi and the burners go down to the black-sand shore under Eyjafjoll to wait on weather and a merchant captain's goodwill. There is no harbour on this coast, only surf and open beach and a ship standing off. They sail in different vessels to different countries, scattering across the Norse world. Kari Solmundarson, who refused the settlement and would take no compensation for his son, sails after them. He is one man against fifteen, with the whole ocean to work in.
suggested_refs: The harbourless black-sand coast under Eyjafjoll
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 146

stops.name: Nidaros, Flosi before Earl Eirik
stops.date_confidence: traditional: Eirik Hakonarson's rule from this region is independently attested in Heimskringla; his particular audience with Flosi is the saga's account alone.
stops.campa: Flosi crosses to Norway and presents himself at the court of Earl Eirik Hakonarson, as Icelanders in trouble have always done, to winter with a great man and come home with his favour attached. The earl receives him. Whatever a pilgrim will have to answer for in Rome, in Norway a burning is a matter between families, and the man who ordered this one eats at the earl's table. News of Kari's landings reaches him there, one name at a time. Fifteen men left Iceland with him. Fewer will go home.
suggested_refs: The court of Eirik Hakonarson at Nidaros, as described in Heimskringla
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 153
Heimskringla, Olafs saga helga (cited at one remove)

stops.name: Birsay, the head on the board
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Coordinate per Wikipedia 'Birsay'; the earl's seat there is traditionally rather than documentarily associated with Sigurd, and the saga puts the Yule feast on Hrossey (Mainland).
stops.campa: At Yule in Earl Sigurd's hall, Gunnar Lambason is asked to tell the story of the burning and tells it as entertainment, mocking the old man's last words for the table. Kari has come in behind the benches unseen. He asks how Skarphedinn bore himself, hears the lie, and takes off Gunnar Lambason's head in one stroke, so that it falls on the board in front of the earl and the blood runs into the laps of Flosi's own kinsmen. Then he walks out of the hall, and out of Orkney, with the earl's men behind him.
suggested_refs: The Yule hall of Earl Sigurd Hlodvisson in Orkney, Dasent ch. 155
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 155

stops.name: Dublin, the promises of Sigtrygg Silkbeard
stops.date_confidence: attested for the coalition and for Sigtrygg's kingship (Annals of Ulster, Wikipedia 'Battle of Clontarf'); the saga's dialogue at his court is invention within a real setting.
stops.campa: Sigtrygg Silkbeard gathers a fleet against Brian Boru and pays for it in promises he cannot keep. He offers the kingship of Ireland and his mother's hand to Earl Sigurd of Orkney, and then offers exactly the same to Brodir of Man, telling each of them not to speak of it to the other. The quays fill with ships out of Orkney, Man, and the Hebrides waiting on the tide. Among the men on them are Icelanders who burned a farm in the Landeyjar three years ago and are still being hunted for it.
suggested_refs: Norse Dublin as the coalition's base before Clontarf
sources: Annals of Ulster, s.a. 1014 (cited at one remove)
Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, chs. 154, 156

stops.name: Caithness, the loom of Darrad
stops.date_confidence: tradition, presented in the saga as fact: no independent witness exists for the vision, and the Darradarljod is a poem the saga incorporates. Kari is placed in Caithness by the saga at the time of the battle.
stops.campa: On the morning of the battle a man named Darrad in Caithness watches twelve riders go into a hillside, and looks in at them through a chink in the wall. Women are at a loom warped with men's guts and weighted with human heads, a sword for the beater and an arrow for the shuttle, and they weave and chant the day's slaughter while it is still happening across the sea in Ireland. Then they tear the cloth apart, each keeping her piece, and mount and ride away. Kari Solmundarson is in Caithness that spring.
suggested_refs: The Darradarljod, the weaving-song of the valkyries, Dasent ch. 157
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 157

stops.name: Clontarf, the raven banner
stops.date_confidence: attested: 23 April 1014, corroborated across Irish, Norse, and Welsh annals. The raven banner is attested in Wikipedia 'Sigurd the Stout'. Kari's presence at the battle is the saga's claim alone, and the saga itself places him in Caithness. The research pool dated the Orkney muster to the day of the battle, which is impossible; the fleet sailed weeks earlier.
stops.campa: The armies meet on the strand north of the Liffey on Good Friday and fight from dawn past midday. Sigurd of Orkney carries a banner sewn with a raven that gives victory to the man it is borne before and death to the man who bears it. Three standard-bearers die under it, no one else will lift it, and Sigurd puts it inside his own coat and is killed. Brian Boru's side wins the field and Brian is cut down in his tent by a fleeing Norseman. The saga folds its Icelanders into the edge of a battle three nations record.
suggested_refs: Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh and the Annals of Ulster on Clontarf, 23 April 1014
sources: Annals of Ulster, s.a. 1014 (cited at one remove)
Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 157

stops.name: Wales, the last of the burners
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no year survives, and the coordinate is a placeholder for Wales rather than a located site. Wikipedia 'Kari Solmundarson' names Wales alongside Orkney as a place where Kari hunted and killed Burners; the research pool's rendering of Wales as an unnamed lord's court where he gathered news is not supported by the text.
stops.campa: Kari's hunt runs through Orkney and down the Irish Sea into Wales, and in Wales it ends. Kol Thorsteinsson is standing in a market counting silver into his own hand when Kari comes up to him, and Kari takes his head off in the middle of the count, and the head says eight before it strikes the ground. That is the last of the men who set fire to Bergthorshvoll. Kari has killed his way through them across four countries, and has nothing left to do with the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The killing of Kol Thorsteinsson in Wales, last of the Burners
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 158

segments.name: Rome, and the Blizzard at Svinafell

stops.name: Rome, absolution for the burning
stops.date_confidence: traditional and internally contradictory: the research pool's chronology lens dates the pilgrimage to 1017, its geography lens to c. 1015-1016. No firm date survives, so one hedged date is carried across this stop and the reconciliation rather than two conflicting ones. The pilgrimage itself is confirmed by Wikipedia 'Kari Solmundarson'; no Vatican record names either man.
stops.campa: Flosi goes to Rome and receives absolution from the Pope himself for the burning. Kari, still outlawed for the killings he did in the hunt, goes to Rome too and receives the same. The two men walk the same roads south a season apart to be forgiven by one authority for opposite halves of a single crime. Iceland's law could not finish this: it produced fines, outlawries, and a brawl on the assembly field. A court eight hundred leagues away, answering to no godord and no Althing, does finish it.
suggested_refs: The Lateran and St. Peter's, goal of Icelandic penitential pilgrimage in the 11th century
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 159

stops.name: Ingolfshofdi, the wreck in winter
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the coordinate is the traditional landfall at Ingolfshofdi and is approximate. Direction of the wreck corrected: Wikipedia 'Kari Solmundarson' has Kari shipwrecked near Flosi's home, not Flosi near Kari's as the research pool's chronology lens had it. Both men had made the Rome pilgrimage, which is the likely source of the confusion.
stops.campa: Coming home from Rome, Kari's ship breaks up on the headland of Ingolfshofdi in winter, and he comes ashore in the worst weather of the year with his crew and no shelter within reach except the one house he has spent five years making an enemy of. Svinafell is the nearest roof under the glacier. He turns inland toward it. He wants a fire and dry clothes for his crew, and in that weather the nearest fire in Iceland belongs to Flosi Thordarson, who ordered the burning.
suggested_refs: The headland of Ingolfshofdi, traditional site of Kari's shipwreck
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 159

stops.name: Svinafell, the guest in the blizzard
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the saga presents this as history and no outside source can confirm or date the reconciliation or the marriage. The research pool dated it to 1018 in one lens and c. 1017 in the other; one hedged date is used.
stops.campa: Kari knocks at Svinafell in the blizzard, and Flosi is on his feet before anyone has said a name, walking out to meet the stranger, and he kisses him and sets him in the high seat. Kari came to test what Flosi would do. Flosi does the only thing that ends it. They are reconciled that night, and Kari afterwards marries Hildigunn, Flosi's niece and Hoskuld's widow, the woman who threw the bloody cloak across Flosi's shoulders and set the burning going. The feud closes inside the family that opened it.
suggested_refs: Svinafell under the tongues of Oraefajokull, Flosi's farm and the saga's last scene
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 159

stops.name: Reykholt, the century that reads it closest
stops.date_confidence: attested for Snorri (c. 1179-1241, killed at Reykholt 1241); the connection to Njal is literary and cultural, not personal. Snorri postdates the saga's setting by two centuries and predates its composition by a generation. Coordinate inherited as the corpus's canonical Reykholt pin.
stops.campa: Two hundred years after the burning, Snorri Sturluson sits at Reykholt with a hot pool outside his door writing the Prose Edda and Heimskringla, codifying the poetic and historical apparatus the saga writers work with. Iceland in his lifetime is tearing itself apart in exactly the manner Njals saga describes: chieftains, kinsmen, arbitration, arson. Snorri will be killed in his own cellar by his son-in-law's men in 1241. The century that reads Njal's story most closely is the century living it again.
suggested_refs: Snorralaug, the hot pool at Reykholt, and Snorri's cellar

stops.name: Iceland, the saga written down
stops.date_confidence: attested as a window, not a year: Wikipedia 'Njals saga' gives composition between 1270 and 1290, and 1280 is the midpoint. The place of composition is unknown; the coordinate is the corpus's canonical Iceland pin. The Vigfusson quotation is restored to its full form, the research pool having softened it.
stops.campa: Somewhere in Iceland between 1270 and 1290 an anonymous writer, learned in law and in poetry, takes two and a half centuries of oral tradition about the Landeyjar and makes the longest of the family sagas out of it. Nobody knows his name. He keeps the lawsuits, the burnings, and the verdicts spoken over graves in the order the tellers before him spoke them, and adds nothing that a court of the old commonwealth could not have heard. Gudbrandur Vigfusson's verdict stands over the book like a gate.
stops.quote: Although it is certain, that Njall has existed, yet the Njall, which Njals saga describes, has never lived.
stops.quote_source: Gudbrandur Vigfusson, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Njall Thorgeirsson'
suggested_refs: Einar Olafur Sveinsson's stemma of 1953 and his standard edition of 1954

stops.name: Copenhagen, the first printing
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia 'Njals saga' for the edition, its editor, its printer, and its manuscript base.
stops.campa: The saga is printed for the first time in Copenhagen, edited by Olafur Olafsson from the Reykjabok vellum with reference to Kalfalaekjabok and Modruvallabok, on Johann Rudolph Thiele's press. Iceland is a Danish dependency, and its medieval literature is being edited, printed, and kept in the capital of the country that governs it. Roughly sixty manuscripts and fragments of this one saga survive, twenty-one of them medieval, hand-copied on Icelandic farms across the four centuries before this press.
suggested_refs: The 1772 Copenhagen editio princeps of Njals saga

stops.name: Edinburgh, the name Burnt Njal
stops.date_confidence: attested: 1861, Edmonston and Douglas, Edinburgh, per Wikipedia 'George Webbe Dasent'. The research pool placed the publication in England, which is wrong.
stops.campa: George Webbe Dasent publishes his English translation with Edmonston and Douglas of Edinburgh and calls it The Story of Burnt Njal. The epithet is his. In Icelandic the book is Brennu-Njals saga and the man is Njall Thorgeirsson; in English he becomes, permanently, Burnt Njal, named for the manner of his death rather than for his father or his farm. Every English reader for a hundred and sixty years meets him already on fire. Dasent's chapter numbering is still the one English scholarship cites.
suggested_refs: The Story of Burnt Njal, Edmonston and Douglas, Edinburgh, 1861, two volumes

stops.name: Thingvellir, Morris at the Law-Rock
stops.date_confidence: attested: william_morris.journey.json records Morris at the Law-Rock in July 1871 naming Njal by his saga role. This is the strongest documented intersection between Njal and any existing traveller in the atlas.
stops.campa: William Morris, who taught himself Old Icelandic in order to translate the family sagas, rides into the rift valley in July and stands at the Law-Rock, and what he writes down is not the geology. Here Njall spoke and Gunnar was outlawed. He has come to Iceland to walk the map of a literature, and the ground answers to the book rather than the other way about. Njal has been dead eight hundred and sixty years and is the reason an English poet is standing in a lava field in the rain, saying his name aloud.
suggested_refs: Morris's Icelandic journals of 1871 and his saga translations with Eirikr Magnusson

stops.name: Bergthorshvoll, the diggers
stops.date_confidence: attested that the excavations happened (Wikipedia 'Bergthorshvoll': Sigurdur Vigfusson in the late 19th century, Matthias Thordarson in 1927, 1928, 1931). Their findings are an explicit gap: the article is a stub and describes no results, and the research pool's claim that archaeology confirms Norse-period occupation on this exact mound overstates what is published.
stops.campa: Sigurdur Vigfusson had already put a spade into the knoll in the last years of the nineteenth century, looking for the fire. Matthias Thordarson, director of the National Museum, comes back in 1927 and again in 1928 and 1931 and digs it properly. Whether what they found under the mound was the saga's burning or the ordinary charring of a thousand years of farmhouses is not stated in anything published that can be reached. The knoll keeps its answer. The farm above it is still worked.
suggested_refs: The excavation campaigns at Bergthorshvoll, late 19th century and 1927-1931

stops.name: Reykjavik, Borges comes to the prose
stops.date_confidence: attested for the visit (borges.journey.json, 1971, with two later returns); the connection to Njal specifically is inferred, since no file records him naming Njal. Coordinate inherited as the corpus's canonical Reykjavik pin.
stops.campa: Jorge Luis Borges, given the Volsunga Saga by his father at ten in Buenos Aires and half a century deep in Old Norse by now, reaches Iceland for the first time at seventy-one. He is nearly blind and has come to stand in the country whose medieval prose he considers a wonder. He will return twice more before he dies, and his gravestone in Geneva will carry a Viking longship and a line from the Volsunga Saga. He never names Njal. Nothing in his own writing records that he read the saga, and nothing records that he did not.
suggested_refs: Borges's Norton lectures on the Eddas and the kenningar, and his Geneva gravestone

stops.name: Reykjavik, Modruvallabok comes home
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia 'Modruvallabok' for the manuscript's date (c. 1330-1370), its provenance through Thomas Bartholin in 1684 and Arni Magnusson in 1691, its custody in the Arnamagnaean Collection, and its return to Iceland in 1974.
stops.campa: The manuscript carrying the largest single collection of Icelandic sagas, written about the middle of the fourteenth century and found at the farm Modruvellir in Eyjafjordur, was handed to the Danish scholar Thomas Bartholin in 1684 and to Arni Magnusson in 1691, and kept in Copenhagen for nearly three centuries. In 1974 it is carried back across the water. Njals saga returns to the island it is about, as an object, in the lifetime of people still farming the Landeyjar it describes.
suggested_refs: Modruvallabok (AM 132 fol.), returned from the Arnamagnaean Collection in 1974

stops.name: Bergthorshvoll, the knoll under grass
stops.date_confidence: present day. The site is identified by unbroken local tradition and farm continuity, not by documentary proof from the burning itself. No memorial stone at the site, and no folklore or hauntings attached to it, could be confirmed from any source reached; both are gaps rather than negations. The Icelandic Saga Centre at nearby Hvolsvollur could not be verified: sagacentre.is failed DNS resolution.
stops.campa: The farm is still worked. The knoll is still there above the Affall, flat land and long sight-lines in every direction, and the road brings people who have read the book and want to see where the hide was spread. Nothing is standing from 1011 and nothing needs to be. Iceland's most famous house is a rise in a field with grass on it, and the country knows to within a few yards where a beardless lawyer lay down with his wife and his grandson and did not get up.
suggested_refs: The mound of Bergthorshvoll today, Vestur-Landeyjar, Rangarvallasysla
sources: Dasent, The Story of Burnt Njal, ch. 132
